newsitem.title: UK: ABN AMRO London fund buy not a big step.
newsitem.headline: ABN AMRO London fund buy not a big step.

text.p: Dutch bank ABN AMRO's plan to buy British fund manager Capel-Cure Myers Capital Management is not the big splash the bank has said it wants to make in the British fund management scene, banking analysts said on Friday.
"With four and a half billion pounds ($6.4 billion) under management this is not a big player," said one analyst.
Capel-Cure Myer specialises in private client stockbroking and fund management rather than institutional funds.

The takeover talks between ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, ABN AMRO's investment banking arm, and Capel-Cure Myers were announced on Thursday. Capel-Cure Myers has 4.5 billion pounds under management and employs around 450 staff.
ABN AMRO has already bought two British fund management firms, Causeway Group and Carrington Pembroke. Both were small and aimed at wealthy private clients rather than institutions.
In January ABN AMRO said it would consider buying a large British fund manager if it fitted in with its strategy.
The bank did not name any targets but the head of its global asset management arm Jan Vroegop told Reuters it would like to make "big steps" in London arena.
But assuming it goes through, the Capel-Cure Myers deal is unlikely to satisfy ABN AMRO's desire to enter the lucrative institutional fund management business.
"ABN is a big bank and its fund management acquisitions have so far been relatively small," a second analyst told Reuters.
"Considering their name has been linked with purchases like Schroders Plc and Mercury Asset Management Group Plc in the past, this is a bit of a different ball park," he added.

Schroders and MAM, although not apparently up for sale at present, have been valued at anything up to 2.5 billion pounds. One analyst suggested Capel-Cure Myers could fetch between 40 and 60 million pounds as it had been on the market for some time and not found a premium buyer.
Analysts said trade buyers seemed to be hanging back from buying into fund management at present as prices were inflated. They suggested some would wait for a bear market.
Fund management is an attractive area for investment banks as the quality of earnings is seen as better than in other areas.
It is relatively low risk, provides stable earnings compared to the more volatile trading activities, demands relatively little capital and is growing fast.

And margins, under pressure in other areas of investment banking as services become industry-wide commodities, remain attractive for those controlling the billions of pounds of pension funds and investment assets now swirling around the mature markets of Britain, the U.S. and Japan.

In January ABN AMRO became embroiled in the Nicola Horlick affair. Horlick, a fund manager with Deutsche Bank's Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), was suspended when it emerged she had been in talks with ABN AMRO.
Horlick later resigned from MGAM amid newspaper reports that ABN AMRO was attempting to poach MGAM staff and back a management buy-out of its British pension fund business.

ABN AMRO has since said it talked to Horlick but denied that it attempted to poach her team. Horlick told Reuters in January that the talks were of "an informal and preliminary nature". ($ = 0.627 British Pounds)
